summary: Page Assist is a browser extension: there is no server and no deployment-wide key, and every LLM call is made with a key the user configured for one provider they chose. So Router is wired in the way this codebase already treats every vendor — as an OpenAI-compatible provider the user adds with their own Router key ("Ramp Router", https://api.router.com/v1) — with the vendored runtime under the OpenAI client translating that provider's chat/completions calls onto Router's /v1/responses, the only generation endpoint Router serves for OpenAI-shaped clients. One Router key then reaches ~100 models across OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Gemini and the open-weight ids from a single provider entry, where today each vendor needs its own entry and its own key; model listing needs no translation because Router serves GET /v1/models in the OpenAI list shape. Two small edits to the vendored runtime make that safe and possible here: it can take its settings from the provider record because process.env does not exist in a browser (process.env still wins where it does), and a wrapped client may only route the hosts it is given, so a request addressed to api.openai.com with the user's own OpenAI key is never diverted to Router. An operator who sets RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY in a build opts api.openai.com and api.anthropic.com in as well, which is the ordinary migration, and that is the path the live checks exercised. Nothing changes for any existing user until they add a Router provider. Verified against the real Router: 11 requests, all 200 — buffered chat, a streamed answer, tool calling, reasoning effort, the model list, and /v1/messages for the Anthropic client — with gpt-5-nano and again with claude-haiku-5-5, including the temperature Page Assist always sends on a model whose catalog rejects it (the runtime drops it). Embeddings, text-to-speech and the Anthropic model list stay on their providers: Router has no endpoint for them. Local Ollama and Chrome's on-device model never involve Router at all, which is the product's whole premise.
reviewed: Read every LLM call path in the product — the seven chat modes, the MCP chat loop, the four retrieval query-rewrite calls, background title generation, embeddings, OCR and TTS — and looked for calls that were wasteful, mislabelled, unguarded, or sending fields no API accepts, as well as for levers Router makes available to this shape of app. Four improvements are built and tested on branches: a reasoning-effort setting that reached the wire as a field no API accepts (so it has never done anything); per-feature spend labels plus a router.policy.json that treats streamed chat, blocking rewrites and background titles differently; a web-search rewrite that ran on the first turn (where it has nothing to resolve) and with images attached to a call that returns a text query; and four retrieval rewrites whose failure cost the user the whole answer. Six more are proposed with no branch, led by the largest cost item in the product — the page or document context sits in the last message of every page-chat turn, which puts it outside any cacheable prefix, so a 10k-token page is charged at full price on every follow-up instead of the measured -90% on Claude and -49% on gpt-4o-mini. That one is a rework: it moves user-editable prompt templates and changes how models see the context, so it needs product sign-off rather than a quiet commit. Shadow models were considered and are recommended against: they need content recording, and PRIVACY.md promises that no data leaves the browser unless the user initiates it.

items.title: Route the OpenAI-compatible chat client through Router
items.summary: The OpenAI client every CustomChatOpenAI instance builds now goes through the vendored runtime, so a chat completion Router can serve is translated onto /v1/responses.
items.gains: One wrap covers every OpenAI-shaped chat call in the product: the seven chat modes, the MCP loop, the four retrieval rewrites and background titles, for the generic OpenAI-compatible, OpenRouter, Vertex and Router providers. Router has no /v1/chat/completions endpoint, so this translation is what makes any of them reachable at all. Streaming, tool calls, structured output and reasoning effort all survive it, and temperature is dropped automatically on the 36 catalog ids that reject it rather than returning 400.
items.loses: nothing
items.price: no change: the runtime is inert until a Router key exists, and routerOptions() then returns {} so the client is byte-for-byte what it was
items.why: Everything else in this migration hangs off this one client construction. The runtime also keeps the escape hatches that matter for a client-side app: a request Router cannot serve exactly (embeddings, audio, images, an unknown model, n>1, logprobs, seed) goes to the original provider unchanged, and a Router refusal before generation (403, 404 model_not_found, an unknown or unsupported parameter) is resent to the provider once. ROUTER_MIGRATE_DISABLE=1 turns the whole thing off.

evidence.detail: 11 requests to the real Router, all 200: buffered chat, a 46-chunk stream, reasoning effort and a tool call, with gpt-5-nano (provider=openai) and again with claude-haiku-5-5 (provider=anthropic)
tsc --noEmit: 16 errors, the same 16 as the pre-migration baseline, none in a touched file
router-migrate check --run: every request reached router-sim as a valid /v1/responses call

items.title: Add Ramp Router as a provider users can select
items.summary: "Ramp Router" joins the provider list with https://api.router.com/v1; the model factory hands that provider's own key to the runtime, and the embedding picker offers nothing for it.
items.gains: One key and one provider entry reach ~100 models across OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Gemini and the open-weight ids, where today a user who wants Claude and GPT and Kimi keeps three provider entries and three keys. Model listing needed no special case — Router serves GET /v1/models in the OpenAI list shape, 100 models live. Router also reports spend per key and per request, which no other provider in this list does.
items.loses: topK, minP and a provider's "custom body" JSON do not apply to Router traffic: Router's Responses surface has no equivalent, and the runtime builds its request from an allowlist, so they are dropped rather than sent and rejected. Router also has no embeddings, audio or image endpoint, so a Router provider cannot serve the knowledge base's embedding model or text-to-speech; the embedding model picker returns nothing for it rather than offering chat models that would 404 at index time.
items.price: the catalog's price for whichever model the user picks, from $0.05/$0.40 per 1M (gpt-5-nano) to $5/$25 (claude-opus-5); billed to the user's own Router key, as every other provider here is billed to theirs
items.why: This is the opt-in that makes the migration real in a browser extension. There is no deployment whose key could be flipped: traffic reaches Router only because a user chose to add Router, exactly as they choose to add Groq or OpenRouter today, and nothing changes for anyone who does not. It also keeps PRIVACY.md's promise intact — no existing provider's traffic moves.

evidence.detail: the full provider path, live: claude-haiku-5-5 served 11 of 11 requests through chat/completions with temperature 0.7 on a model whose catalog says temperature:false (the runtime dropped it), plus 100 chat models listed and 0 embedding models offered
router-migrate levers against the live catalog: claude-haiku-5-5 $0.10/$0.50, gpt-5-nano $0.05/$0.40, claude-sonnet-5 $2/$10, gemini-2.5-flash $0.30/$2.50, grok-4.7 $2/$6, gpt-oss-120b $0.15/$0.60
16 errors, the baseline's 16

items.title: Let an operator build route the Anthropic Messages client
items.summary: CustomChatAnthropic's raw fetch to api.anthropic.com/v1/messages goes through the runtime, which sends it to Router's /v1/messages when a Router key is in the build environment.
items.gains: Completes the migration for anyone who builds the extension with RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY set — an enterprise or self-hosted build where the operator, not the end user, owns the key. The dated model id the app sends (claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929) is mapped to the catalog id, and the x-api-key already on the request means a Router refusal before generation falls back to Anthropic once.
items.loses: nothing
items.price: catalog price on Router instead of Anthropic list price; the two matched exactly in Router's own measurements
items.why: The scanner calls this a handoff because it is raw HTTP rather than an SDK, but the runtime's fetch handles POST /v1/messages directly, so routing it needed one call site changed instead of a rewrite onto the Anthropic SDK. In the extension this stays on Anthropic: the key comes from a provider record the user filled in with their Anthropic key, so routerRouteHosts() does not list api.anthropic.com and their traffic is untouched. Requests carrying an anthropic-beta header stay on Anthropic either way — this class sets interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14 whenever a thinking budget is set, and beta features through Router are unmeasured.

evidence.detail: 200 on /v1/messages, model=claude-haiku-5-5, provider=anthropic, feature=src/models/CustomChatAnthropic.ts:anthropicFetch; the reply came back through the class's own SSE parser unchanged
16 errors, the baseline's 16
router-migrate check --all still reports this site as "stays": its static scan cannot see that anthropicFetch is the runtime. The live /v1/messages request above is what settles it.

items.title: Label every call by feature, and give each feature its own policy
items.summary: pageAssistModel takes a feature name, sends it as Router's spend label, and router.policy.json then treats streamed chat, blocking rewrites and background titles differently.
items.gains: Spend becomes readable per feature instead of arriving as one undifferentiated label (every request previously reached Router as "src/models/CustomChatOpenAI.ts:<module>"), and the policy can then act per feature: chat.* get a prompt_cache_key, so the page or document context that leads those prompts is a cache hit on later turns — measured on Router at -49% for a 9,020-token gpt-4o-mini prompt and -90% for a 10,362-token Claude one; the blocking *.rewrite calls get service_tier "default", because Router's account default is the cheaper Flex tier, which may queue (a measured Flex call took 61 s) and nothing is on screen until a rewrite returns; title gets a cross-vendor candidate list so a background title still gets written when the chosen model is unavailable.
items.loses: The *.rewrite calls give up the Flex discount — they are short, so this costs cents. A title can come from claude-haiku-5-5 rather than the model the user picked, if theirs is unavailable. Router ignores allow_flex_tier beside a candidate list, so title keeps the account default tier rather than an explicit one. The label is sent only on Router traffic, so no other provider sees a new header.
items.price: net saving: the cache key applies to the largest prompts in the product, the tier change applies to the smallest
items.why: This is the change that turns Router from a proxy into a control plane for this app, and it is what every other per-feature decision needs first. The three kinds of work here have genuinely different requirements — a streamed answer the user is reading, a buffered call that blocks the UI, and a fire-and-forget background title — and until they were labelled, Router could not tell them apart. Note for whoever applies this: i3 and i4 touch the same lines in searchChatMode.ts and useMessage.tsx, so apply this one first.

evidence.detail: 11 live requests, all 200, with the labels visible per request in Router's own view (feature=chat, feature=websearch.rewrite, feature=title); run twice, with gpt-5-nano and with claude-haiku-5-5

bodies recorded off the wire: chat -> prompt_cache_key=chat, provider_timeout=180, metadata.product=page-assist; websearch.rewrite -> service_tier=default, provider_timeout=20; title -> models=[the chosen model, the fallback]

new measurement, listed as unknown in the fact sheet: service_tier "default" and provider_timeout on a Claude model over /v1/responses both returned 200 (claude-haiku-5-5), and a cross-vendor candidate list [claude-haiku-5-5, gpt-5-nano] was accepted and served by anthropic
16 errors, the baseline's 16

items.title: Put page and document context first, so it can be cached
items.summary: Move the retrieved context out of the last human message into a stable system message, so a follow-up turn's prompt shares a cacheable prefix with the one before it.
items.gains: This is the largest cost and latency item in the product. Chatting with a page sends the whole page — routinely 5,000 to 50,000 tokens — and today it is substituted into the last human message together with the question (`systemPrompt.replace("{context}", context).replace("{question}", message)` in the tab, knowledge-base, document and chat-with-page modes), so it moves to the end of the prompt and changes every turn. Nothing before it is big enough to cache, so the page is charged at full input price on every single follow-up. With the context as a leading system message and only the question varying, the prefix is identical turn to turn: Router measured -90% on a 10,362-token Claude prompt and -49% on a 9,020-token gpt-4o-mini one, and cached reads are a tenth of input price in the catalog (claude-sonnet-5 $0.20 against $2.00). Time to first token falls with it. The web-search mode already has this shape — its results go in a system message and the human message is just the question — which is a useful reference for what the other four should look like.
items.loses: Models weight system and user content differently, so answers will change in ways that need judging rather than asserting; some local models handle a long system message worse than a long user message. The prompt templates carrying {context} and {question} are user-editable and ship with saved user values, so existing customised prompts need a migration or a compatibility path. Caching only pays above roughly 1,024 tokens of identical prefix, so short pages gain nothing.
items.why: The saving is large and applies to the product's headline feature, but it changes prompts users can edit and answers users will notice, which is a product decision rather than a quiet commit. Proposed rather than built for that reason. The honest first step is one mode (tabChatMode) behind a setting, compared side by side on real pages, before the other three follow.

items.title: Send reasoning effort as a field the APIs actually accept
items.summary: CustomChatOpenAI sent the Reasoning Effort setting as `reasoning: { method }`, which no API takes; it now sends `reasoning_effort`.
items.gains: A setting that is exposed in two places in the UI starts working. OpenAI, Groq, OpenRouter, DeepSeek and vLLM all read `reasoning_effort` on Chat Completions, and the runtime maps it to Responses' `reasoning.effort` for Router — only on models whose catalog entry says they reason, and on Claude only when there is room to think, so no request gains a field its model would reject. On a strict provider the old field was worse than inert: OpenAI rejects an unrecognised body field outright, so setting reasoning effort could fail the request.
items.loses: Requests that previously carried the ignored field now carry a real one, so a model that supports reasoning will actually spend tokens reasoning when the user asks it to — slower and dearer on those turns, which is what the setting is for.
items.price: more output tokens on turns where a user deliberately asked for reasoning effort
items.why: A visible setting that silently does nothing is worse than no setting, and this one is three lines. The fix is confirmable rather than arguable: before, the translated request carried reasoning=undefined from params {"reasoning":{"method":"low"}}; after, reasoning={"effort":"low"}.

evidence.detail: same assertion on both sides of the change: before, translated reasoning=undefined; after, reasoning={"effort":"low"}
live on Router, gpt-5-nano at effort low answered 17*23 correctly (200, provider=openai); all other live checks still passed
16 errors, the baseline's 16

items.title: Stop the web-search rewrite running first-turn, and with images
items.summary: Both web-search paths skip the follow-up rewrite when there is no prior turn to resolve against, and never attach images to a call whose output is a search query.
items.gains: Removes a whole generation from the critical path of every first web search — it was the only thing between pressing send and the search starting, with nothing on screen — and stops paying for every attached screenshot as vision input (run through OCR first, when OCR is on) on a call that returns a string. The three other retrieval modes already skip the rewrite in exactly this case, and the web-search path in useMessage.tsx had the same `newMessage.length > 2` guard sitting commented out above it, so this also removes an inconsistency rather than inventing a rule.
items.loses: On a first-turn search the query is the user's own words rather than a keyword-ified version of them ("What are the symptoms of a heart attack?" instead of "heart attack symptoms"), and a first-turn search of an image alone no longer gets a model-written query. Follow-up turns rewrite exactly as before.
items.price: one fewer generation per first web search, and no image tokens on any rewrite
items.why: The rewrite prompt's entire job is to resolve a follow-up against the conversation it follows. On the first turn there is no conversation, so the call was spending the user's slowest seconds restating a question that had nothing to resolve. Apply after i2, which touches the same lines.

evidence.detail: 16 errors, the baseline's 16

reasoned from the code, not from a sample: on a non-regenerated first turn newMessage is [user, placeholder], so chat_history was the empty string and the prompt's {chat_history} slot was blank. The latency and token saving follows from the call not being made; no quality comparison was run on the keyword-ification that is given up.

items.title: Don't lose the answer when the retrieval rewrite fails
items.summary: The knowledge-base, tab, document and chat-with-page rewrites fall back to the raw question instead of letting an error kill the turn.
items.gains: A timeout, a rate limit or a refusal on an auxiliary call stops costing the user their answer. Retrieving with the user's own words works perfectly well — it is what the web-search path has always done on failure, since that one call has been wrapped in a try/catch all along. It is also what makes a short provider_timeout safe to set on these features in router.policy.json: the timeout then degrades the query instead of killing the turn.
items.loses: A rewrite failure is now silent apart from a console error, where it previously surfaced as an error message. The retrieval that follows uses a less well-formed query, so the answer may be slightly worse rather than absent.
items.why: Four modes had the call bare inside the mode's outer try, so an error on the cheap preparatory step propagated to saveMessageOnError and the user got an error instead of an answer. One of the five sibling modes already had the guard; the inconsistency is the bug. Apply after i2, which touches nearby lines in the same files.

evidence.detail: 16 errors, the baseline's 16

read from control flow: in ragMode, tabChatMode, documentChatMode and useMessage's chatWithWebsiteMode the invoke sat inside the mode's outer try with no catch of its own, while searchChatMode wraps the same call and falls back to `message`

items.title: Run rewrites and titles on a cheap model, not the chat model
items.summary: Extend the existing title-generation model setting to the five retrieval rewrites, defaulting to a small fast model when the provider is Router.
items.gains: The rewrites and the title are mechanical, short-output jobs that currently run on whatever the user picked for conversation — which may be claude-opus-5 at $5/$25 per 1M, or a local 70B model that takes ten seconds to load. gpt-5-nano is $0.05/$0.40 and claude-haiku-5-5 is $0.10/$0.50, so a Router user's utility turns get 50-100x cheaper and noticeably faster, on exactly the calls that block the UI. The product already has the mechanism and the UI pattern for this: titleGenerationModel. Router is what makes it practical — one key already reaches a cheap model, so the user does not have to configure a second provider to get one.
items.loses: A small model resolves pronouns and context less reliably, so some follow-up queries will be rewritten worse, and a user who deliberately chose one model now has two models in play. Needs a settings surface and a sensible default, including for users with only a local Ollama model, where a second model means a second load.
items.why: Clear win on cost and on the latency the user feels most, but it needs a product decision about the default and a settings surface, and the quality of a small rewriter should be sampled on real follow-ups before it becomes the default rather than asserted here.

items.title: Decide whether interactive chat should leave the Flex tier
items.summary: Add service_tier "default" to the chat.* entries in router.policy.json, trading the Flex discount for a predictable first token.
items.gains: Removes the queueing risk from the calls a user is watching. Router's account default is cost-efficient routing, so a Page Assist answer is served at Flex unless asked otherwise, and Flex may queue: one measured gpt-5-nano Flex call took 61 s. A sidebar that stalls is a sidebar people stop opening.
items.loses: The Flex discount on the product's largest calls — exactly -50% where it was measured (gpt-5.4-mini), and unmeasured on every other model. This is real money on long page-chat prompts, and it is the user's own money.
items.why: i2 deliberately made this call only for the short blocking rewrites, where the discount is worth cents and the latency risk is total, and left streamed chat on the account default. Streaming gives chat some protection — the docs describe an implicit 25 s deadline on a streamed Flex attempt before a same-model standard fallback — but 25 s of nothing is still a bad answer. Whether to pay roughly double for the main answer is a judgement about this product's users, not a bug, so it is written up rather than decided: the change is three words per feature in router.policy.json and is reversible.

items.title: Say something when the output cap is too small to answer
items.summary: When a reasoning model returns nothing because the user's max-token setting was spent on reasoning, tell them that instead of showing an empty reply.
items.gains: Turns a blank, unexplained answer into a message a user can act on. This is observed, not theoretical: live on Router, gpt-5-nano with a 64-token cap returned an empty reply twice, and the same prompt at 400 tokens answered normally. Page Assist's default leaves the cap unset, so only users who set one are affected — but Ollama users set numPredict as a habit, and carrying that habit to a reasoning model produces silence.
items.loses: nothing in behaviour; it needs a new user-facing string, so translations for the extension's locales.
items.why: Cheap and purely additive, but it is a UI and i18n change across the chat modes' streaming loops rather than a model-layer fix, which is why it is proposed rather than committed. Raising the cap behind the user's back would be the wrong fix: it spends their money on a limit they set deliberately.

items.title: Count tokens with Router instead of a local OpenAI tokenizer
items.summary: Use Router's free /v1/messages/count_tokens for context accounting instead of CustomChatOpenAI's bundled OpenAI tokenizer.
items.gains: getNumTokens counts with an OpenAI tokenizer whatever the model is, so the numbers it produces for Claude, Gemini, Kimi, DeepSeek and the rest are wrong — and they are what decides how much page content gets trimmed into a prompt (maxWebsiteContext) and what the UI reports. Router's count_tokens is free, costs no spend, and is exact for Anthropic-served models and estimated otherwise, with the header x-router-token-count-source saying which.
items.loses: A network round trip where there was local arithmetic, so it needs caching and a local fallback when offline — and the local path has to stay for Ollama and Chrome's on-device model, which never touch Router. Router also reports token counts of its own that are known wrong for some Fireworks-served models, so the result needs sanity bounds.
items.why: Right-sizing page context is the difference between a truncated page and a 400, and today it is guessed with the wrong tokenizer. Worth doing, but it adds a network dependency to a code path that is currently synchronous and offline, so it wants a design rather than a patch.

items.title: Try Switchyard for the chat model, once a strategy is saved
items.summary: Offer `model: "switchyard"` so Router picks a cheap or a capable model per turn within one conversation.
items.gains: A sidebar conversation is mostly easy turns with occasional hard ones, which is the shape Switchyard is built for: it switches model family within a conversation, cheap model for easy turns and capable model for hard ones, and it worked from app code in Router's own measurements. For a user who would otherwise pick one expensive model for everything, this is the single biggest lever on their bill that does not require them to think about it.
items.loses: Different turns are answered by different models, so tone and formatting shift inside one conversation, which is visible in a chat UI. Router's docs call it experimental and aimed at coding agents, and its quality on non-coding work is unmeasured. It also needs a human to save a routing strategy (efficient_model and capable_model) on app.router.com before the model id does anything, so it cannot ship as a default.
items.why: Promising and cheap to try, but it depends on an account setting this repository cannot make and on quality that nobody has measured for conversational use. The honest path is an opt-in model entry labelled experimental, tried by someone who can watch their own bill and answers.

items.title: Embeddings stay on their provider
items.summary: OAIEmbedding keeps calling the provider's /v1/embeddings: Router has no embeddings endpoint, and no catalog model is an embedding model.
items.gains: none
items.loses: nothing
items.why: Router's /v1/embeddings returns 404 and the live catalog (100 models) contains no embedding model, so the knowledge base, document chat and chat-with-page retrieval keep whichever embedding provider the user configured. The runtime leaves these requests alone by design. The one change made for them is defensive: a Router provider offers no embedding models in the picker, so nobody selects a chat model there and discovers the problem at index time.

items.title: Text-to-speech stays on its provider
items.summary: openai-tts keeps calling the provider's audio endpoint: Router serves no audio.
items.gains: none
items.loses: nothing
items.why: Audio is not in Router's endpoint list, and audio input on /v1/responses returns 400 "Audio input is not available". The same holds for the ElevenLabs and Mistral speech paths, which are not OpenAI-shaped at all. Worth noting for support: pointing the TTS base URL at Router would 404, and nothing in the UI stops a user doing that.

items.title: Each provider's model list stays with that provider
items.summary: getAllAnthropicModels and the Google, Vertex and OpenRouter list paths keep going to their own vendors.
items.gains: none
items.loses: nothing
items.why: Router serves GET /v1/models, but only its own catalog — it cannot answer "which models does this user's Anthropic key have". Each provider's list therefore stays with that provider, and a Router provider lists Router's catalog (verified live: 100 models). The runtime also leaves model-list requests on the provider by design.

items.title: Local and on-device models never involve Router
items.summary: Ollama chat and embeddings and Chrome's built-in Gemini Nano keep talking to localhost and to the browser.
items.gains: none
items.loses: nothing
items.why: This is the product's premise — "use your locally running AI models" — and these calls never leave the machine. ChatOllama talks to the Ollama HTTP API, which is not an OpenAI-shaped endpoint, and Chrome's model runs in the browser with no HTTP at all. Routing either one would mean sending a user's page content to a gateway when they specifically chose not to send it anywhere, so neither is touched, and neither appears in the scanner's list. Named here so it is on the record that the majority of this extension's traffic is, by design, not on Router.

items.title: Gemini through Google's own endpoint stays there
items.summary: The Google AI and Vertex providers keep using Google's OpenAI-compatible endpoints rather than Router's Gemini ids.
items.gains: none
items.loses: nothing
items.why: Router's 24 Bedrock and Vertex ids are requires_byok: Gemini returns 403 provider_key_required without the caller's own Google credential. A user who configured the Google AI provider already has that credential pointed at Google, so routing their request through Router would cost a round trip and a 403 before the runtime resent it to Google anyway. Gemini is still available to a Router provider for anyone who attaches their Google key to their Router account — it is just not something to do on their behalf.

items.title: Two hand edits to the vendored runtime, and why
items.summary: routerRuntime.ts was edited twice: settings can come from the app, and a wrapper can be limited to named hosts.
items.gains: none
items.loses: nothing
items.why: The outside check flags a hand-edited runtime, so here is exactly what changed and why neither edit alters behaviour on any path the runtime was built for. Edit 1 (setRouterEnv, and env() falling back to it): there is no process.env in a browser extension, so the Router key and base URL can also be supplied at runtime from the provider record; process.env still wins wherever it exists, which is every node path — tests, `check --run`, an operator build. The alternative was injecting a fake `process` global into the extension, which would have changed how bundled libraries detect their runtime. Edit 2 (RouterOpts.routeHosts, three lines in planRequest): a wrapper can be told the exact hosts it may route. Page Assist holds one key per user-configured provider, so without this a Router key would have diverted requests addressed to api.openai.com with the user's own OpenAI key. When routeHosts is absent the behaviour is identical to the vendored original. Both edits are commented in place and marked "page-assist edit n of 2". src/libs/routerPolicy.ts is generated by `router-migrate policy` from router.policy.json (on the i2 branch), not written by hand.

items.title: Shadow models: recommended against for this product
items.summary: Router's shadow models need content recording, which conflicts with the extension's privacy promise.
items.gains: none
items.loses: nothing
items.why: Shadow models would be a natural fit otherwise: they record cost and latency for up to three candidate models on a sample of real traffic, which is exactly the evidence i6, i7 and i9 are missing. But they require content recording to be on, and PRIVACY.md states that no data is transmitted to external servers unless the user explicitly initiates it, and that the extension integrates with no analytics. Recording a sample of users' page content on Router's side to tune model choice would break that, and it is the kind of thing that costs an extension its reviews. If the question needs answering, the right way is a local A/B with the user's own consent, or an operator running shadow models on their own non-consumer build. Spend caps per key are worth mentioning to users for the opposite reason: a Router key is the one key here that can be capped, which is a real safety net for a browser extension holding a billing credential.
